notes: Under the CTO's A71 ruling of 10/1, local-serving sales respond to the town's pay with Moretti's long-run elasticity, 0.335, and the response builds over time instead of landing in full each quarter. It builds on the outcome web's half-life shape (acuteWeight), with half the gap closing in TOWN_FINANCE_POLICY.business.localDemandHalfLifeDays, set by hand at 1,095 days.
Moretti measures the response over census decades (1980 to 1990 and 1990 to 2000), so the full response is a ten-year one; how fast it arrives within those ten years is not measured there.
question: After a lasting change in a town's tradable employment or payroll, how fast do its local-serving businesses' sales or jobs follow: what share of the long-run response arrives in the first year, by three years, and by ten?

sourcesChecked.source: Moretti, Local Multipliers, AER Papers and Proceedings 100(2), 2010
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Ten-year changes only; no path within the decade.

sourcesChecked.source: Nguyen and Soh, Employment Multipliers over the Business Cycle, World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 8105, 2017
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Reports year-by-year county offsets of job changes, not the build-up of local-serving sales toward a long-run elasticity; not converted.

title: How fast a town's local sales catch up with its pay
usableAnswer: The share of the long-run local-serving response realized at one, three and ten years after a lasting local payroll change (or a half-life), from a named study using county or metro panels, so the half-life can be read as data rather than set by hand.
whyItMatters: It decides whether a plant closing or a raise shows on main street within a season or over years, which is what a player watching the town after their law sees.
